region: Eastern North America; introduced and invasive in parts of Europe
description: Black cherry is a fine-grained North American hardwood that darkens from pinkish brown to a deep reddish brown with light exposure. It is a favorite for furniture, cabinetry, turning, and small boxes.

hazards.summary: IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancer of the nasal cavity and sinuses after long-term heavy exposure. This applies to every species, so dust control matters whatever you cut.

exposure_limits.note: 8-hour time-weighted average, as restated by OSHA

related_species_note: 'African cherry' in asthma literature (Obata 2000) is makore (Tieghemella heckelii), not Prunus. Schlunssen-2018 lists sweet cherry (Prunus avium) under unspecified 'allergy', citing German-language sources we could not verify.

Fine, even texture with straight grain, a few small dark gum flecks and faint wavy figure, tiny diffuse pores, and a smooth satiny luster. No text, no logos, no hands, no tools, no finish or varnish, natural unfinished wood. Wide 1200x630 composition (1.91:1) with the board centered and margin on both sides for cropping.

notes_internal: No species-specific reports found. PubMed searches on 2026-11-07: 'Prunus serotina' with dermatitis/asthma/allergy/occupational/dust/wood/toxic; 'cherry' in title with wood/sawdust and asthma/rhinitis/dermatitis/allergy; 'cherry wood'. Only hit was Obata 2000 (makore, mislabelled African cherry). Not in HSE-WIS30 table. ACGIH puts it in the A4 'all other wood dusts' group (not species-named, so no level 2 entry). Leaves, bark and seeds of Prunus serotina contain cyanogenic compounds (livestock poisoning literature), which is not a wood-dust hazard and was not added. The page should state clearly that no species-specific reports were found and that this is not evidence of safety. Absence of reports for a hazard is not evidence that this wood is safe.
